column1: F001|Include a view from the normal entrance, one facing the proposed position and a detail of any obstruction. Explain where each photograph was taken and what normally occupies the area. Keep addresses, family photographs and other unnecessary private details outside the frame. Photographs help explain the brief; they do not confirm dimensions or suitability.|/commission

F002|Use both when they answer different questions. A whole-room view explains the relationship to doors, seating and existing objects; a closer view can show the proposed position or a specific constraint. Label their relationship on a simple sketch. Avoid sending several near-identical close-ups that leave the surrounding space unclear. Keep measured facts separate from visual estimates.|/commission

F003|Describe when the room is used, where daylight enters and which artificial lights are normally on. A pair of photographs from the same position at different times can help explain the change. Note curtains and weather where relevant. Do not treat camera brightness or screen colour as an exact measurement of the room's lighting conditions.|/commission

F004|Yes, a simple labelled sketch can explain a proposed position and nearby openings. Include units for any measurements, a reference corner and a note identifying estimates. Distinguish existing features from proposed outlines. The sketch is a discussion aid; it does not become an approved manufacturing or installation drawing merely because it accompanies the brief.|/commission

F005|Include the furniture and objects that will remain relevant to the proposed piece. Explain whether their position is fixed and what relationship matters: use, outline, colour or visibility. You do not need a complete household inventory. A favourite existing object may be a useful reference without requiring the new piece to match every material or detail.|/commission

F006|Label the locations A and B on the same sketch and provide a contextual photograph of each. Explain the advantage and unresolved question for each option. Keep the proposed object assumptions consistent so the comparison is understandable. Neither location should be treated as confirmed until the relevant dimensions, access and intended use have been reviewed.|/commission

F007|You can begin with the room's purpose and an open question through the custom-piece brief. Describe the activity, proposed position and what you would like to improve or explore. Add a small number of relevant references. This starts a conversation; it does not confirm a room-design service, feasibility, a quotation or a production booking.|/commission

F008|Describe the main activities and any different priorities among the people using the space. Identify which choices are shared and which remain unresolved. A consolidated brief is useful when the actual decision-makers have reviewed it. Do not present one person's preference as everyone's agreement or assume a generic layout meets every user's needs.|/commission

F009|Leave out details unnecessary to the design discussion, such as visible addresses, private documents, family photographs and identifying views through mirrors. Check the background as carefully as the main subject. Share only references you are entitled to provide. Private inquiry references are not automatically public catalogue images or permission to publish a room story.|/privacy

F010|Choose a few words and explain each with a visible example. “Quiet” might mean a simple outline rather than a pale colour; “warm” might describe a relationship between materials rather than a specific hue. State which interpretation matters and add the room's practical use. The description is a preference for discussion, not an exact specification.|/commission

F011|Start with the proposed position's width, depth and relevant height, plus nearby openings or fixed obstructions. State units, the date and whether the values are approximate. Distinguish room measurements from desired object dimensions. The atelier will need to discuss the actual design and access before initial numbers can become a confirmed specification.|/commission

F012|Initial estimates can help explain an idea if they are clearly labelled approximate. Record how and when they were obtained and identify what still needs checking. Do not remove the qualification when copying the numbers into another message. Final dimensions require recorded approval; an estimate in a saved inquiry is not that approval.|/terms

F013|Use a consistent unit and write it explicitly, such as centimetres or millimetres. Put it in the drawing title and beside any value that could be ambiguous. Avoid mixing units without labels. Identify what each arrow measures and whether it concerns the room or the proposed object. Clear notation does not replace checking the measurements.|/commission

F014|Doorways and the route to the proposed room can be relevant, not just the room itself. Record the opening direction, approach and nearby turns or obstructions where you can do so safely. These observations support an access discussion. They do not guarantee that a piece will fit through or that installation is available at the destination.|/shipping-delivery

F015|Identify lift entrances, internal space, staircase turns, landings and any known building restrictions. Pair photographs with a simple route sketch and label uncertain measurements. Do not attempt risky access trials. Delivery and installation arrangements are reviewed individually; installation is available only by prior arrangement within Surat under the current delivery policy.|/shipping-delivery

F016|Give the photograph a reference and show its location on a sketch. State units and the endpoints of each measurement. Mark estimates clearly and include the date. Keep the original image if you annotate a copy. A labelled photograph explains where a number belongs but does not independently verify that the measurement is accurate.|/commission

F017|Final design and dimensions require recorded approval before work begins. The brief should identify who supplied the site measurements and which values still need verification. Do not assume a polished drawing or a website submission has already confirmed them. Ask the atelier how the final specification and any site checks will be agreed for your request.|/returns-cancellations

F018|Describe the unusual shape with a labelled sketch and contextual photographs. Mark the reference edges, openings and any areas whose dimensions are uncertain. Explain the intended use before suggesting a solution. This provides material for a feasibility discussion; it does not confirm that a particular form, size or installation method can be supplied.|/commission

F019|Tell the atelier which location has changed and identify the existing inquiry or proposal. Review dimensions, access, lighting and surrounding objects for the new position. State which preferences should carry over. A location change may affect the discussion, so do not assume the earlier specification or delivery arrangement automatically applies to the new room.|/commission

F020|No. A visualization communicates an appearance or proposed arrangement, not verified finished dimensions. Perspective and cropping can make proportions difficult to judge. Use the confirmed dimensioned specification for the actual piece and keep approximate sketches labelled. If an image and a written dimension seem inconsistent, ask for clarification before approving the proposal.|/terms

F021|Place the two outlines in the same room sketch at a stated scale, or clearly label the comparison approximate. Explain whether you are comparing edge shape, visual mass or relationship to nearby objects. Keep other differences from distracting from that question. The comparison supports discussion; it does not confirm construction, fit or practical suitability.|/commission

F022|Describe how the pair should relate and what each piece is intended to do. Identify shared features and intentional differences, such as height or colour emphasis. Do not assume that a visual pair can nest, stack or support one another. Those functional details, along with feasibility and the final specification, need separate confirmation.|/commission

F023|Different viewpoints are helpful when they reveal different information. A whole-object view can explain proportions, while a side view may show an edge or opening hidden from the front. Label which feature matters in each. Several photographs of the same source remain one reference or project, not evidence of several completed commissions.|/portfolio

F024|Describe the feature creating that impression: a narrower outline, more visible empty space, a quieter colour relationship or a less dominant position. Add a reference and explain the specific part you mean. “Lighter-looking” is a visual preference; it does not establish actual weight, stability, construction or the suitability of a proposed design.|/commission

F025|A paper outline or mock layout can help compare positions and proportions. Label the scale, units and assumptions, and explain which question it tests. Keep any physical marker out of normal movement routes. The exercise does not represent height, weight, stability or real access, so final dimensions and practical suitability still need review.|/commission

F026|Mention the objects that affect use or composition: nearby seating, doors, fixed fittings, wall art and pieces that must remain. Explain which positions are fixed and which may change. Include the relationship that matters rather than listing everything in the room. Existing objects are references, not automatic instructions to duplicate their materials or finish.|/commission

F027|Show the whole wall and its relationship to furniture, openings and the normal viewing position. Mark the proposed composition on a copy of the photograph or a sketch. Explain the intended visual anchor. Keep mounting suitability, fixing methods and installation arrangements as separate questions; a balanced-looking image does not establish any of those facts.|/shipping-delivery

F028|Yes, if the alternatives are clearly labelled and their differences are explained. Give each a reference, contextual image and unresolved question. State whether you prefer one or want advice about both. Avoid combining measurements from different options into a single apparent specification. The final position and design must be agreed separately.|/commission

F029|Describe the variation in a product or custom-piece request and identify the catalogue reference that inspired it. Explain what you want to retain and what you would like to change. That starts a feasibility discussion; it does not edit the public catalogue product or confirm that every requested variation can be made.|/commission

F030|No. An inspiration image communicates a direction and may omit important context about materials, dimensions or construction. State which feature interests you rather than requesting an unexplained identical result. The collection uses design visualizations, and final details are agreed individually. Do not infer a finished appearance or performance guarantee from the image alone.|/faq

F031|Use visible relationships: clear beside opaque, a narrow blue accent beside grain-like lines, or a quiet edge around a stronger centre. Explain which relationship matters most and provide a contextual reference. Keep technical properties as questions unless supported by confirmed information. A description of appearance does not identify composition, certification or a care method.|/materials-care

F032|No. A photograph may show colour, pattern and apparent texture, but it cannot certify composition, species, finish or performance. Ask for the relevant material details for the actual proposed piece. Keep the visual reference separate from any specification or supporting document so that an attractive image is not mistaken for technical evidence.|/materials-care

F033|Viewing angle, lighting, reflections and the surrounding room can change how a surface appears in photographs. Compare contextual views and describe what differs without diagnosing the cause from one image. If the difference matters to the proposal, ask for clarification. The photographs alone do not establish a change in material or finish.|/materials-care

F034|Usually both are useful because they answer different questions. The close-up can show a boundary or pattern, while the wider image shows where it belongs and how prominent it is. Label the detail's location and purpose. Without reliable scale information, a macro photograph should not be used to infer the physical size of the feature.|/materials-care

F035|Describe the visible direction, spacing and contrast of the grain-like pattern, then explain which quality you prefer. Keep colour as a separate observation if it is important. Do not identify a timber species or origin from appearance alone. Any confirmed material identity belongs in the actual specification and supporting source information.|/materials-care

F036|Yes. Explain what you mean visually, such as seeing background shapes through an area or preferring a more solid-looking colour field. Use a whole view and detail if they help. A photograph's apparent transparency does not establish optical quality, thickness, ageing behaviour or another material property; those remain specific questions for the proposal.|/materials-care

F037|No. Glossy-looking highlights may reflect lighting and image treatment as well as a surface. Describe the reflection quality you like, then ask how the finish would be specified and reviewed for the actual piece. Do not infer coating type, durability, cleaning instructions or a guaranteed result from a polished-looking reference photograph.|/materials-care

F038|Keep confirmed material details with the current agreed design and specification, clearly separated from inspiration images and early preferences. Identify the version and any later clarification. If a detail is still unknown, leave it as a question instead of filling it in from a similar-looking product. Approval concerns the actual proposed piece.|/terms

F039|You can ask whether a sample discussion or another way of reviewing the material direction is appropriate for your request. Explain what uncertainty you want to resolve, such as colour relationship or apparent finish. Do not assume a sample service, availability, cost or exact matching guarantee from this question; those need individual confirmation.|/commission

F040|Look at the stated classification and source, not just how realistic the image appears. A design visualization can explain a concept but cannot prove a material property or completed installation. For a factual claim, ask what evidence relates to the actual piece. Keep unverified identity, certification and performance claims out of the brief.|/materials-care

F041|Yes, as a starting reference. Include the source where known, mark the area that interests you and explain the intended colour relationship in words. Screenshots can be affected by the original image, processing and display. They do not establish an exact finished match, so the final colour direction needs separate discussion and approval.|/commission

F042|Context is helpful when the relationship to walls, flooring or existing objects matters. Label the surroundings that will remain and explain whether the aim is contrast, similarity or a small accent. A cropped swatch alone may not communicate that intention. Photographic context still does not make the reference a calibrated colour sample.|/commission

F043|Displays, image processing and viewing conditions can make the same image look different. Treat the screenshot as a discussion reference and describe the effect you want in ordinary words. Avoid choosing a final specification solely by comparing uncalibrated screens. Ask how the actual proposed colour and finish will be reviewed before approval.|/materials-care

F044|Label one reference as the primary direction and explain why. Put supporting references and alternatives in separate groups. Identify the exact feature that matters so the reader does not assume every colour in the image is requested. A clear priority helps the discussion but does not guarantee material availability or an exact match.|/commission

F045|Several options can be discussed if they are clearly labelled as alternatives. Explain what changes between them and what should remain consistent. Keep each palette with its intended room or use context. Do not combine all alternatives into one apparent instruction; the final agreed direction should identify which option and version were selected.|/commission

F046|No. A colour code can identify a reference, but it does not by itself guarantee how the finished material will look under different conditions. State the source of the code and the intended visual relationship. Confirm how colour expectations, material variation and the actual proposal will be reviewed before treating the choice as agreed.|/materials-care

F047|Keep both images and note their sources and known conditions. Explain the difference you see and which appearance you prefer. Ask for clarification tied to the actual proposed piece instead of assuming one image is wrong or that the finish changed. Differences in light, angle or processing may be relevant but should not be guessed as fact.|/materials-care

F048|Yes. Describe the room's usual daylight and artificial lighting and provide contextual photographs if useful. Ask about the appearance of the actual proposed material and finish in relevant conditions. The answer should not be inferred from a generated room scene. A lighting discussion also does not establish technical exposure limits or placement suitability.|/materials-care

F049|Record the agreed direction with the current proposal or specification, including the relevant reference and version. Keep earlier options marked superseded rather than allowing them to look equally current. A personal preference note or a saved website brief is not itself agreement. Ask for clarification if written notes and the current proposal appear inconsistent.|/terms

F050|Explain what should remain quiet and what may stand out. You might prefer a narrow accent, lower contrast against nearby colours or a softer relationship between patterned and plain areas. Add a whole-object reference so the scale of the effect is clear. “Muted” alone does not specify a colour, finish or exact outcome.|/commission

F051|Describe the purpose, proposed position or occasion, leading preferences and the questions you want to discuss. Include only a few relevant references and identify what each explains. Check your contact details and exact personalization text before saving. The saved brief starts an inquiry; feasibility, quotation, payment arrangements and delivery are agreed separately.|/commission

F052|Use separate labelled sections for the room idea and the keepsake idea. Explain whether they are related or independent, and identify the different references and questions for each. Do not assume a room measurement applies to the keepsake or that one feasibility answer covers both. Ask how the atelier would like the discussion organized.|/commission

F053|A small set with clear reasons is usually more useful than many unexplained images. Choose references that answer different questions, such as outline, colour relationship and placement. The current inquiry upload accepts up to three JPG, PNG or WebP images, each up to 3 MB. Label alternatives so they are not read as simultaneous requirements.|/faq

F054|Use separate lists and give each must-have a reason. Distinguish verified site constraints from desired design responses. Mark optional ideas and unresolved questions clearly. This makes it easier to preserve the purpose if a preferred solution is unsuitable. Calling something essential does not confirm feasibility; the final design still needs discussion and recorded approval.|/commission

F055|You can provide an architect-prepared brief as relevant context. Identify its author, date, version and which measurements or proposals it contains. Keep site facts separate from preferences and make the decision-making roles clear. The brief does not automatically establish a partnership, installation commitment or accepted specification; those arrangements need individual discussion.|/architects

F056|Give each question a short label, explain why it matters and identify who may be able to answer it. Put questions that affect other decisions first. When an answer arrives, record its source and date. Leave unresolved items visibly open rather than converting a tentative response or silence into an approved detail.|/commission

F057|A consolidated summary can reduce contradictions when the actual decision-makers have reviewed it. Collect comments against the same proposal version and preserve unresolved differences. Agree who will communicate the summary where appropriate. Do not create several duplicate inquiries simply to repeat one brief, and do not imply consent from someone who has not reviewed the choices.|/contact

F058|Keep a private copy of important wording while preparing it; do not assume every unsaved form field will be recovered later. When the website reports a successful save, the inquiry is recorded and a message can be opened or copied. Saving does not send WhatsApp automatically or confirm the order. Review the receipt before the handoff.|/faq

F059|Use a clear title, date and version, with a short note describing what changed. Maintain one index pointing to the current reference set and keep superseded ideas labelled. Distinguish a brief version from an approved specification or quotation. A file named “final” does not establish that the atelier has accepted its contents.|/commission

F060|Use the custom-piece brief to describe the idea and ask whether it is feasible. State the purpose, relevant constraints and the uncertainty you want resolved. Existing page examples and visualizations are references, not promises of every possible service or variation. Wait for an individual discussion before assuming availability, price, timing or a production booking.|/commission
